steps.text: Integral calculus is the inverse of differential calculus – and at the same time a tool for computing areas, distances and quantities. At university it comes early and fast. If you master the standard techniques securely, you'll have a much easier time.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. Antiderivatives: finding the "anti-derivative"
2. The definite integral and the fundamental theorem
3. Substitution and integration by parts
4. Applications: areas, means, distances
steps.insight: Integrating means: recovering the total change from the rate of change – distance from velocity, function value from slope.

steps.text: An antiderivative of \(f\) is a function \(F\) with \(F' = f\). It is determined only up to an additive constant.
steps.explanation:
Why \(+C\)? Constants vanish when differentiating: \((x^2 + 5)' = (x^2 - 3)' = 2x\). All these functions are antiderivatives of \(2x\).

The most important antiderivatives:
\(\begin{array}{c|c} f(x) & F(x) \\ \hline x^n & \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \ (n \neq -1) \\ \frac{1}{x} & \ln|x| \\ e^x & e^x \\ \sin x & -\cos x \\ \cos x & \sin x \end{array}\)

The check is always possible: differentiate and compare with \(f\). \(\int x^4\,dx = \frac{x^5}{5} + C\), since \(\left(\frac{x^5}{5}\right)' = x^4\) ✓.
steps.insight: The special case \(n = -1\): \(\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C\). The power rule would divide by \(0\).

steps.text: Sum and factor rules also hold for integration. Roots and fractions are first written as powers.
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \(\int \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \int x^{-2}\,dx = -x^{-1} + C = -\frac{1}{x} + C\)
• \(\int \sqrt{x}\,dx = \int x^{1/2}\,dx = \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\)

Linear substitution (inner function \(ax + b\)): integrate as usual and divide by \(a\):
• \(\int (2x + 1)^3\,dx = \frac{(2x + 1)^4}{4 \cdot 2} + C = \frac{(2x + 1)^4}{8} + C\)
• \(\int e^{3x}\,dx = \frac{e^{3x}}{3} + C\)
• \(\int \cos(2x)\,dx = \frac{\sin(2x)}{2} + C\)

Dividing by \(a\) is the counterpart of the inner derivative in the chain rule.
steps.insight: Check by differentiating: \(\left(\frac{e^{3x}}{3}\right)' = \frac{3e^{3x}}{3} = e^{3x}\) ✓. Without dividing by \(3\) a wrong factor would result.

steps.text: The definite integral measures the area under a curve. The idea: cut the area into narrow rectangles and let them become narrower.
steps.explanation:
The animation shows \(f(x) = x^2\) on \([0, 2]\): with \(4\) rectangles you get \(1.75\), with \(8\) already \(2.19\), with \(64\) about \(2.60\). In the limit you get \(\frac{8}{3} \approx 2.667\).

This is how the Riemann integral is defined: as the limit of the sums. In practice, though, one doesn't compute like this but with the fundamental theorem.
steps.insight: The sums \(\sum f(x_k)\,\Delta x\) are the ancestors of the integral sign: \(\int\) is an elongated "S" for "sum".

steps.text: The fundamental theorem of calculus connects both worlds: the definite integral is computed with an antiderivative.
steps.explanation:
The animation shows why: the area function \(A(x) = \int_0^x f(t)\,dt\) grows at the point \(x\) by a narrow strip of height \(f(x)\). Its rate of change is therefore \(f(x)\) – \(A\) is an antiderivative of \(f\).

Example: \(f(t) = 1 + \frac{t}{2}\): \(A(x) = x + \frac{x^2}{4}\). \(A(1) = 1.25\), \(A(2) = 3\), \(A(3) = 5.25\).

Calculation examples:
• \(\int_0^2 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3}\)
• \(\int_1^2 (2x + 1)\,dx = [x^2 + x]_1^2 = 6 - 2 = 4\)

The constant \(C\) drops out: \((F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a)\).
steps.insight: Upper limit minus lower limit – in that order. Swapping the limits flips the sign: \(\int_b^a = -\int_a^b\).

steps.text: The integral is an ORIENTED area: parts below the \(x\)-axis count negative. For the actual area you must split at the roots.
steps.explanation:
\(f(x) = x^2 - 1\) has the root \(x = 1\):
• On \([0, 1]\): \(\int_0^1 (x^2 - 1)\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} - 1 = -\frac{2}{3}\) (below the axis, negative).
• On \([1, 2]\): \(\left[\frac{x^3}{3} - x\right]_1^2 = \left(\frac{8}{3} - 2\right) - \left(\frac{1}{3} - 1\right) = \frac{4}{3}\) (above the axis).

The integral over \([0, 2]\) is \(-\frac{2}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = \frac{2}{3}\); the area between curve and axis is \(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = 2\).

Extreme example: \(\int_0^{2\pi} \sin x\,dx = 0\), because positive and negative parts cancel – but the area is \(4\).
steps.insight: The question "area?" means: find the roots, integrate interval by interval, add the absolute values.

steps.text: The area between two curves is computed as the integral of the difference: upper graph minus lower graph.
steps.formula: A = \int_a^b \big(f(x) - g(x)\big)\,dx \quad \text{for } f \ge g \text{ on } [a, b]
steps.explanation:
Example: \(f(x) = x\) and \(g(x) = x^2\) intersect at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\); in between \(f\) is on top:
\(A = \int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6}\).

Procedure: (1) find intersections by equating, (2) check which graph is on top, (3) integrate the difference.

Second example: \(x^2\) and \(2 - x\): intersect at \(x = -2\) and \(x = 1\) (from \(x^2 + x - 2 = 0\)). In between \(2 - x\) is on top:
\(\int_{-2}^1 (2 - x - x^2)\,dx = \frac{9}{2}\).
steps.insight: Draw a sketch: it shows which graph is on top and prevents sign mistakes.

steps.text: Substitution is the reverse of the chain rule: you replace an inner expression by a new variable.
steps.formula: \int 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx: \quad u = x^2,\ du = 2x\,dx \ \Rightarrow \ \int e^u\,du = e^{x^2} + C
steps.explanation:
Telltale sign: the integrand contains a function \(g(x)\) AND (up to a constant factor) its derivative \(g'(x)\).

Recipe:
1. Choose \(u = g(x)\), form \(du = g'(x)\,dx\).
2. Write everything in terms of \(u\) and integrate.
3. Substitute back (for an indefinite integral).

Examples:
• \(\int x(x^2 + 1)^3\,dx\): \(u = x^2 + 1\), \(du = 2x\,dx\), so \(x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}du\). Result \(\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{u^4}{4} = \frac{(x^2 + 1)^4}{8} + C\).
• Definite: \(\int_0^2 \frac{x}{x^2 + 1}\,dx\): \(u = x^2 + 1\), limits \(u(0) = 1\), \(u(2) = 5\): \(\frac{1}{2}\int_1^5 \frac{du}{u} = \frac{1}{2}\ln 5 \approx 0.805\).
steps.insight: For definite integrals substitute the limits too – then you save the back-substitution.

steps.text: Integration by parts is the reverse of the product rule:
steps.explanation:
Choose \(u\) so that \(u'\) becomes simpler, and \(v'\) so that it is easy to integrate.

• \(\int x\,e^x\,dx\): \(u = x\), \(v' = e^x\): \(x e^x - \int e^x\,dx = x e^x - e^x + C = e^x(x - 1) + C\).
• \(\int \ln x\,dx\): \(u = \ln x\), \(v' = 1\): \(x\ln x - \int x \cdot \frac{1}{x}\,dx = x\ln x - x + C\).
• \(\int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x + C\).

With limits: \(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx = \big[e^x(x - 1)\big]_0^1 = 0 - (-1) = 1\).

Rule of thumb for choosing \(u\) (LIATE): Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic (polynomials), Trigonometric, Exponential.
steps.insight: Always check by differentiating: \(\big(e^x(x - 1)\big)' = e^x(x - 1) + e^x = x e^x\) ✓.

steps.text: Integrals over unbounded regions or singularities are called improper. They are defined as limits.
steps.explanation:
\(\frac{1}{x^2}\) decays fast enough: the infinitely long area has finite content \(1\) (convergent). \(\frac{1}{x}\) decays too slowly: the area grows beyond all bounds (divergent).

In general: \(\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\) converges exactly for \(p > 1\).

Also \(\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx = \left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_0^1 = 2\) is improper (singularity at \(0\)) and convergent.
steps.insight: Infinitely long doesn't mean infinitely large – a foretaste of the convergence of series and integrals.

steps.text: Applications: the integral of the rate of change is the total change. And the mean value of a function is an integral divided by the length of the interval.
steps.explanation:
• Distance from velocity: \(v(t) = 3t^2 + 2\) m/s. Between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 4\): \(s = [t^3 + 2t]_0^4 = 64 + 8 = 72\) m.
• Flow quantity: rate \(r(t) = 10 - 2t\) L/min for \(0 \le t \le 5\): \(V = \int_0^5 (10 - 2t)\,dt = [10t - t^2]_0^5 = 25\) L.
• Mean value of \(x^2\) on \([0, 3]\): \(\frac{1}{3}\int_0^3 x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 9 = 3\).

Unit check: \(\text{m/s} \cdot \text{s} = \text{m}\). The integral multiplies the unit of the function by the unit of the variable.
steps.insight: The mean value \(\bar{f}\) is the height of a rectangle over \([a, b]\) that has the same area as the graph.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Antiderivative: \(F' = f\), \(+C\). \(\int x^n = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\), \(\int \frac{1}{x} = \ln|x|\), \(\int e^x = e^x\), \(\int \sin = -\cos\), \(\int \cos = \sin\).

2. Fundamental theorem: \(\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)\). Integral = oriented area. Area: split at the roots.

3. Area between curves: top minus bottom.

4. Substitution (\(g\) and \(g'\)), substitute the limits too. Integration by parts \(uv - \int u'v\).

5. Improper integrals as limits. Applications: distance, quantity, mean value.
steps.insight: Congratulations! In "Integral Calculus" you learn the Riemann integral precisely, in "Multidimensional Calculus" multiple integrals. The techniques from here remain the foundation.
